pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Ignores changes that only affect the timestamp in the managed fields. That can happen when someone merely updates a Quantity from 1024 to 1Ki or when accidentally removing a value that was a default. This change will reduce the total number of writes to etcd for usages which apply frequent changes to configuration with no semantic value.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:

Usage: `Fixes #<issue number>`, or `Fixes (paste link of issue)`.
_If PR is about `failing-tests or flakes`, please post the related issues/tests in a comment and do not use `Fixes`_*
-->
Fixes #95460

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
NONE
```

issue_context.title: Server Side Apply causing spurious resourceVersion bumps on no-op patch
issue_context.body:
**What happened**:

Running `kubectl apply --server-side -f tmp.yml` with 

```yaml
apiVersion: keda.k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: dummy-0-6
  namespace: pipeline
spec:
  cooldownPeriod: 600
```

the generation, resource version, and managedFields timestamp all change even when running it multiple times in a row (i.e. when the apply should result in no changes).

The relevant via of the CRD from KEDA 1.4.1 is:

```yaml
              cooldownPeriod:
                format: int32
                type: integer
```

**What you expected to happen**:

No change to resource version (or generation or managedFields timestamp) is expected.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

```
kubectl get scaledobject -n pipeline dummy-0-6 -o yaml > old.yml
kubectl apply --server-side=true -f tmp.yml
kubectl get scaledobject -n pipeline dummy-0-6 -o yaml | diff -u old.yml -
```

**Anything else we need to know?**:

This may be related to #94275. I tried manually editing the CRD to format `int64` and `int` but still saw the issue. Applying non-`int32` fields in the same object does not show the same behavior.

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):

```
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"17", GitVersion:"v1.17.3", GitCommit:"06ad960bfd03b39c8310aaf92d1e7c12ce618213", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2020-02-13T18:08:14Z", GoVersion:"go1.13.8", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"darwin/amd64"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"17+", GitVersion:"v1.17.9-gke.6300", GitCommit:"eb6985a7ebfd53457b0b91ba08fac07597bb87af", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2020-09-15T09:20:11Z", GoVersion:"go1.13.9b4", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
```

- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: Server is GKE.

You can find the CRD for this version of KEDA at https://github.com/kedacore/keda/blob/v1.4.1/deploy/crds/keda.k8s.io_scaledobjects_crd.yaml. Reproducing it didn't require actually running the KEDA controller, it was 100% just on the apiserver side.

The statefulset re-generating a new resourceVersion is a different bug but we can keep it here for now.

What happen is that the volumeClaimsTemplate is an atomic list with defaulted fields. Anytime the statefulset is applied, the list of claims is "changed" (defaults are removed), causing the managedfields timestamp to be updated, even though the defaults end-up being re-added causing a no-op.

Daniel and I discussed how we could address that by looking at the actual changes before the object is persisted.

> Anytime the statefulset is applied, the list of claims is "changed" (defaults are removed), causing the managedfields timestamp to be updated, even though the defaults end-up being re-added causing a no-op.

I share @liggitt 's concerns that, while code-wise being clean now, this fixup logic still feels misplaced. Why does SSA even update the managed fields timestamp (my take below)? Why do we need this fixup code being put in every update/patch code path, even without SSA being involved?

To understand, this is the order:
1. SSA does its thing
2. mutating admission runs
3. defaulting runs
4. the resulting object migth be unchanged compared to oldObj, while step (1) saw a change?

In other words, this transformer fights against an SSA patch that is continuesly trying to fight against some admission plugin or default. E.g. a mutating admission plugin sets `spec.privileged=false` for security policy reasons, but a GitOps system insists on `spec.privileged=true`. The result without this PR would be a hot loop with constantly updated managed fields timestamp.

One maybe important detail for a questionable gut feeling: 

This logic uses semantic equality, which is uncommon elsewhere in the storage stack. What if we used normal, deep equality?

Then this would turn into:

a mutating admission plugin sets `spec.extraPermissions=[]` for security policy reasons, but a GitOps system insists on `spec.extraPermissions=undefined`. The result without this PR would be a hot loop with constantly updated managed fields timestamp.

On the other hand, with this PR in place we would miss actual changes in etcd (where a mutating webhook sets undefined to `[]`) where the managedField is not updated. That's the source of the bad gut feeling I guess.

> Why does SSA even update the managed fields timestamp (my take below)? Why do we need this fixup code being put in every update/patch code patch, even without SSA being involved?

Because we don't want to track defaults/mutation changes as part of SSA so we run at the very beginning, but it also means that we don't know know what these changes are going to be and if they will undo a change.

> To understand, this is the order:
> 1. SSA does its thing
> 2. mutating admission runs
> 3. defaulting runs
> 4. the resulting object migth be unchanged compared to oldObj, while step (1) saw a change?

Yes, that's correct. Step 1 doesn't know what step 2 and 3 will do and specifically doesn't want to track these changes. But specifically when 2 and 3 undo what 1 saw, then we want to skip the extra etcd write (hence 4).

> The result without this PR would be a hot loop with constantly updated managed fields timestamp.

That's correct, that's the problem we're trying to solve here, and it's causing actual pain to users.

> This logic uses semantic equality, which is uncommon elsewhere in the storage stack. What if we used normal, deep equality

Note that this comparison is not by-passing any write to etcd. The only action it takes now is to by-pass the update to the timestamp in the managed fields.

We can not use deep equality because deep equality doesn't work for structures that have unexported fields.
In order to make it work, we had to copy the whole semantic deepequal (which doesn't do anything but provide custom comparison for kubernetes types that have unexported fields: https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/blob/master/pkg/api/equality/semantic.go#L29-L49). It also doesn't do anything specific for `undefined to []`.

> On the other hand, with this PR in place we would miss actual changes in etcd (where a mutating webhook sets undefined to []) where the managedField is not updated.

No, because we're not changing the object or preventing the object from going to etcd, we're just reverting the timestamp change. So if there is a change in the object, it's still going to go to etcd. If there is a change to managed fields other than the timestamp, it's still going to go to etcd.

We're only comparing the timestamp, any change in ownership will always be preserved.
